newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: El Nino seen hitting Australian farm exports.
newsitem.headline: El Nino seen hitting Australian farm exports.

text.p: A cyclical warming of the Pacific Ocean known as the El Nino effect will slash Australia's next wheat crop by over 30 percent from last season's record harvest, government forecasters said on Tuesday.

In its quarterly commodities bulletin, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) cut its forecast for wheat production to 16.25 million tonnes from its previous forecast of 19.2 million tonnes.
The 1996/97 wheat harvest, when farmers enjoyed near-perfect weather and prices were firm, was a record 23.6 million tonnes.

But drought conditions exacerbated by the El Nino pattern developing off South America would contribute to a five-percent fall in the value of farm exports to A$20.2 billion (US$15.2 billion), said the government's chief commodity forecasting unit.

ABARE still predicted 3.9-percent growth in overall commodities exports to A$60.8 billion, with minerals and energy both seen strong, but the weak farm sector forced it to ditch a previous prediction of 7.3 percent export growth for the year to June 30.
Estimated total export growth this financial year was put at 2.6 percent for an export value of A$58.5 billion.
"Lower winter crop production, and hence lower exports of grains, is a major factor in the forecast fall in farm exports," ABARE said in a statement accompanying its report.

"Crop yields are forecast to be below average in the eastern states, reflecting the (Australian) Bureau of Meteorology's announcement that it is confident an El Nino weather pattern will persist for the remainder of the year.
"With yields well below last season's record, the wheat crop is forecast to be down about 30 percent to 16.2 million tonnes despite plantings being little changed."
Mineral resource exports were forecast to rise by nine percent to A$38.2 billion, with world prices for most metals seen rising strongly over the remainder of 1997 and in 1998.
ABARE said the star performer among the metals would be nickel, with a world price up 15 percent. Aluminium was seen rising by eight percent and zinc by 12 percent.

The most notable exception was gold. Citing market uncertainty caused by Swiss and German moves to sell down official reserves, ABARE forecast its price forecast for 1997/98 to US$352 to US$375. Gold is currently trading around US$342.
ABARE forecast a seven-percent rise in the world price of crude oil.
So far Australian grain farmers have refused to get too excited over El Nino, which can have a profound effect on global weather patterns for as long as 18 months.
ABARE said its grain production forecasts were in any case based on a less disruptive El Nino effect than those in 1994 and 1982, when world grain crops plummeted.

The dry weather, which will also affect production in North America and Europe, was seen contributing to an expected six-percent rise in local wool prices and a nine-percent rise in saleyard prices of cattle.
But ABARE said that if drought persisted in eastern and southern Australia, farmers could be forced to send sheep and cattle herds to slaughter -- sending prices downwards.
